title: Ryokan and the thief
hookLine: the poet-monk wishes he could give the thief the moon in his window
carry: I wish I could give the moon

lines: A THIEF IN AN EMPTY HUT.
THE MONK GIVES HIM HIS CLOTHES.
cards: A small hut on a hillside in Japan belongs to an old monk who owns almost nothing. One night a thief slips in, searches every corner, and finds nothing worth taking. Then the monk comes home and catches him.
The thief freezes. The monk, the story goes, isn't angry. He's sorry.
You came all this way, he says, and there's nothing here for you. So he takes off his own clothes and hands them over. The thief grabs them and runs into the dark.
The monk sits down in his empty doorway and looks up at the moon.

teach.b: It's a story people tell about Ryokan, a Zen monk and poet who lived simply, begging for his food in nearby villages.
Tradition remembers him in a hut with a begging bowl, not at the head of a temple, and the thief story fits everything else people remember about him. First, the gift.
Ryokan doesn't defend what little he has, and he doesn't lecture. He sees a man who came looking for something and is about to leave with nothing, and that seems to bother him more than the loss.

teach.h: HE GIVES THE THIEF HIS CLOTHES.
teach.b: His clothes are the only thing worth giving, so he gives them.
Buddhist teaching calls giving dana, and treats it as a practice, not only a kindness: something you do on purpose, again and again, until the hand opens more easily. Second, the moon.
After the thief is gone, tradition says, Ryokan wrote a very short poem.

teach.h: THE MOON LEFT IN THE WINDOW.
teach.b: In plain English it runs something like: the thief left it behind, the moon in my window. He wished, the story goes, that he could have given the man the moon too.
In the poem, the one thing worth having couldn't be carried off. Third, an ordinary day. A thief may never come to your door, but small takings do: a seat, a parking space, the credit for an idea.
Ryokan's story doesn't ask how to get it back.
It asks what's still in the window that nobody could take, and whether you could give a little more than was taken.

how: Ryokan's poems and the stories told about him are read in Zen communities and beyond as pictures of a simple, generous life, and Buddhist teaching names giving, dana, as a practice to cultivate.

games.q: you're Ryokan. you come home to find a thief in your hut, and there's nothing in it to take. what do you do?
o: give him the clothes you're wearing.
games.why: in the story Ryokan is sorry the man came for nothing, so he hands over his own clothes, then sits and looks at the moon.

practice: Look around at what's near you and choose one thing you could give away, a book, a jacket, an hour of your time, a kind word you've been holding back, and, if you like, who it's for.
Notice the small tug of wanting to keep it, and breathe with it without fighting. Then let your eyes rest on something open, a window, the sky, a light, something nobody can take from you.
